title: Power, Politics & Organizational Influence
question: If the organization chart does not show who can make change happen, what does — and how should a leader use that knowledge without corroding the trust the organization runs on?

overview.text: Every organization has two architectures. The formal one is drawn on the chart: titles, reporting lines, decision rights. The real one is made of dependence, relationships, coalitions and legitimacy, and it decides whether a well-designed change is used or quietly ignored. This week is about the second architecture, studied with the tools of organizational sociology and social psychology rather than with folk wisdom about “office politics”.

You will move from the individual to the field. Lesson 1 explains where power comes from: the bases that targets perceive, and the dependence relations that create them. Lesson 2 maps informal networks — weak ties, brokers across structural holes, the difference between who is consulted and who is trusted — and weighs the causal evidence behind network claims. Lesson 3 treats organizations as coalitions embedded in fields that reward legitimacy, and examines co-optation, the most common way of buying support, together with its hidden price. Lesson 4 turns to influence without authority: which tactics produce commitment, how to sell an issue upward, what the persuasion research does and does not support after the replication crisis, and where persuasion becomes manipulation.

The work of the week is practical. In the Influence Map you will rate the power, interest and stance of ten people in a fictional hospital system adopting a contested change, and compare your read with the author’s. The case places you in a city government trying to build an office that four organizations must cooperate to make work. The assignment asks you to write a stakeholder engagement plan for a change of your own choosing — by default, a new analytical or operational process in a sports organization — with particular attention to implementing an improvement without undermining existing relationships.

Two cautions run through the week. First, much of what managers believe about power and influence comes from practitioner books and vivid cases; you will learn to separate that material from the research beneath it. Second, the same knowledge that lets you build a coalition lets you manipulate one. You will be asked, repeatedly, to say where your own lines are.

objectives: Analyze where power sits in an organization using the bases of power and the power-dependence relation, distinguishing formal authority from practical power.
Map informal advice, trust and communication networks and identify brokers, single bridges and hidden power holders.
Explain organizational change as the renegotiation of a political coalition and evaluate co-optation and legitimacy strategies, including their costs.
Select influence tactics for upward, lateral and downward influence based on the evidence, and judge persuasion research by its replication record.
Design a stakeholder engagement plan that sequences conversations, sets concessions and states explicit ethical lines.

lessons.title: Where Power Comes From: Bases, Dependence and the Chart That Lies
lessons.summary: Power is a relation of dependence, not a line on an organization chart, and you can map where it actually sits before you try to change anything.
objectives: Distinguish authority, power and influence, and classify a claim to power by its base.
Analyze a workplace situation with the power-dependence formula: importance, discretion and alternatives.
Explain why formal authority and practical power diverge, and predict where they will.
Evaluate the practitioner status of “managing with power” advice against the underlying research.
lessons.executive: Formal authority is the power the organization lends you; practical power comes from what others depend on you for. French and Raven’s five bases — reward, coercive, legitimate, expert, referent — describe how targets perceive an agent. Resource dependence theory explains where those perceptions come from: people who control something important, with discretion over it, and for which there are few alternatives, gain power regardless of title. Before proposing a change, map who depends on whom. Expect power to sit where uncertainty is handled. Remember that dependence runs both ways: your boss and your peers depend on you too, and that mutual dependence is the raw material of influence.

explore.text: A regional hospital system decides to roll out a new electronic early-warning score for patients whose condition is deteriorating. The chief medical officer signs the policy. The chief nursing officer endorses it. The vendor trains every unit. Six months later the score is computed for every patient and acted on in two units out of eleven. When the quality team investigates, the explanation is not a technical failure. In the units where the score works, a respected night-shift charge nurse decided it was worth using and told her colleagues so; in the others, experienced nurses quietly continued to rely on their own judgment, and no one with a title noticed until the data came in.

Every executive has seen a version of this story. A decision is made at the top of the chart and then dissolves somewhere below it. The usual diagnosis — “poor communication”, “resistance to change”, “culture” — names the symptom rather than the cause. The more precise question is: who actually controlled whether this change would happen, and why did the people who signed the policy not control it?

Before reading on: list the three people in your own organization whose cooperation would be hardest to replace if you wanted to change a core process. For each, write down what exactly you would depend on them for. Is it their approval, their knowledge, their relationships, their time, or their example?

This lesson gives you two tools for answering that question. The first is a vocabulary for the *bases* of power — the reasons a person complies with another. The second is a structural theory, resource dependence, that explains why power accumulates where it does. Together they show why the organization chart is a partial and sometimes misleading map of who can make things happen.

understand.title: Prerequisite: authority, power and influence — three words managers blur

blocks.text: **Power** is the capacity to affect what others do, including when they would prefer otherwise. **Influence** is power in use: the actual change in someone’s behavior, beliefs or decisions. **Authority** is power that people accept as legitimate because of a position or a rule — the right to direct, recognized by those who are directed. Sociologists since Max Weber have treated legitimacy as the feature that turns raw power into authority. The distinction matters because authority is granted by the formal structure, while power can come from anywhere, and influence is what you are actually trying to produce.

Two further distinctions help. Power is **relational**: it exists between particular people over particular matters, not as a quantity someone carries around. And power is **potential**: a person who never uses it may still shape outcomes, because others anticipate what that person would do.

understand.text: The bases of power

In a short chapter published in 1959, the social psychologists John French and Bertram Raven proposed that interpersonal power rests on a few distinct bases. Their crucial move was to define each base from the point of view of the person being influenced. **Reward power** exists when the target believes the agent can provide things the target values. **Coercive power** exists when the target believes the agent can punish. **Legitimate power** rests on the target’s acceptance that the agent has a right to direct — the base that formal authority provides. **Referent power** rests on identification: the target wants to be like, or be liked by, the agent. **Expert power** rests on the target’s belief that the agent knows more about the matter at hand. Raven later added a sixth base, informational power — influence through the content of a persuasive argument itself rather than the standing of the person making it.

French and Raven also noted that the bases behave differently. Coercive power requires surveillance, because compliance lasts only while the agent can observe and punish, and it tends to reduce the target’s attraction to the agent. Expert power has a limited range: a surgeon’s expertise gives her influence in the operating room, not over the hospital’s parking policy. Referent power can operate without the agent being present at all, because the target carries the model around.

understand.text: Power as dependence

French and Raven describe how power feels to the target. They say less about why some people end up with more of it. The structural answer comes from sociology. In power-dependence theory, the power of A over B equals B’s dependence on A. Jeffrey Pfeffer and Gerald Salancik built that idea into resource dependence theory, which they applied to whole organizations: an organization depends on another actor to the degree that the resource the actor controls is **important** to it, the actor has **discretion** over its allocation and use, and there are **few alternative sources**. Where all three are high, dependence is high, and with it the potential for external control.

understand.caption: From a resource to power: the dependence chain

steps.label: Importance
steps.text: How critical is it — would the work stop or degrade without it?

steps.label: Power
steps.text: The controlling actor can shape decisions — whether or not it holds formal authority.

understand.text: Pfeffer and Salancik’s central claim is that much of what organizations do can be read as the management of dependence. Organizations bring powerful outsiders onto their boards, form alliances and joint ventures, merge with suppliers or buyers, and diversify their sources — all ways of reducing the leverage that someone else holds over them, or of absorbing it. The same logic applies inside an organization. Units that supply something other units critically need, and that cannot easily be replaced, gain influence over budgets and decisions out of proportion to their place on the chart.

Return to the hospital. The policy carried legitimate power. But adoption depended on something the night-shift charge nurses controlled: the judgment of whether the score was clinically credible on a busy ward, and the example that less experienced nurses followed. That resource was important (no one acts on a score they do not trust), the charge nurses had discretion over it (no policy can mandate trust), and there was no alternative source (the vendor’s trainers had no standing on the ward). By the dependence formula, the charge nurses held more practical power over adoption than the chief medical officer.

understand.caption: Formal authority versus control of a critical dependency
cells: **Peripheral.** Little leverage on this decision; often a useful informant because others overlook them.
**Hidden power holder.** The charge nurse, the database administrator, the veteran scout. Change succeeds or fails here; engage early and personally.
**Nominal authority.** Can sign the decision but cannot make it happen; risks overestimating its own reach.
**Concentrated power.** Authority and dependence coincide; the decisive actor for this change — but also the one most likely to be overconfident about compliance below.
understand.note: Teaching device. Position each actor for a specific decision; the same person can sit in different cells for different decisions.

challenge.text: Both frameworks have limits you should know before relying on them. The French and Raven typology was proposed on theoretical grounds, not derived from data, and its categories overlap in practice: a manager’s legitimate power usually comes bundled with reward and coercive power, and expert power often becomes referent power over time. Because each base is defined as a belief held by the target, it is hard to measure without asking targets, and their answers mix perception, liking and memory. Treat the typology as a diagnostic vocabulary, not as a set of separate levers with known effects.

Resource dependence explains who *could* exercise power better than how they *will*. A department that controls a critical resource may choose not to use its leverage, may not realize it has leverage, or may be constrained by norms. Pfeffer himself has argued, in work written for managers, that many capable people fail at implementation precisely because they are uncomfortable acquiring and using power, and that discomfort leaves the field to others. *Managing with Power* is a practitioner synthesis — research-informed, built on organizational cases, but not a test of its own prescriptions — and you should read its advice in that light.

There is also a normative objection. If power is the ability to prevail over others’ preferences, then advising managers to accumulate it can reward political skill over substance and erode trust. The structural view does not settle this; it only describes. In Lesson 4 you will see evidence that the tactics through which power is used matter a great deal for whether people commit or merely comply, and you will build explicit ethical lines into your own engagement plan.

challenge.title: Methodological note: why power is hard to measure

blocks.text: Researchers have used three broad strategies to locate power in organizations and communities, and each has a characteristic blind spot. **Positional** approaches read power from formal roles; they miss hidden power holders by design. **Reputational** approaches ask informants who is powerful; they capture perception, which matters, but they also capture visibility and status, and they can be self-fulfilling. **Decisional** approaches trace who prevailed on actual contested decisions; they are the most behavioral but miss power that keeps issues off the agenda altogether, or that operates through anticipation — people not proposing what they expect a powerful actor to veto. Mid-twentieth-century debates about community power were largely debates among these three methods.

For an executive the practical implication is to triangulate. Ask who has the title (positional), who people say matters (reputational), and who has actually won or blocked the last three comparable decisions (decisional). Where the three answers diverge, you have found the interesting part of the organization. Notice also what never reaches a decision at all: proposals that die before being made are evidence of power too.

apply.text: Consider four hypothetical settings. In a software company, the platform team that runs the deployment pipeline has no authority over product teams, but every release depends on it, and building an alternative pipeline would take a year: its views on engineering standards carry weight far beyond its headcount. In a law firm, a partner who personally holds the relationships with three major clients has power over firm policy that the managing partner’s title does not match, because those clients are important, the relationships are hers to direct, and they cannot be easily moved. In a military staff, the officer who controls the flow of information to the commander — which reports are summarized, which are attached, which arrive first — holds influence that the organization chart describes only as “staff support”. In a city government, the budget office’s discretion over mid-year transfers makes department heads attentive to its analysts’ preferences.

Notice that in each case you can name the resource, rate its importance, identify who holds discretion and count alternatives. That is the skill: making dependence explicit instead of sensing it vaguely. It also points to strategies. You can increase your power by controlling something important (building a capability others need), by increasing discretion, or by reducing others’ alternatives — and you can reduce someone else’s leverage over your project by creating alternatives, sharing the resource, or making the dependence mutual.

In a professional baseball organization the same analysis applies. The coordinator whom players trust holds referent and expert power that a front-office mandate cannot replace; if a new development process requires that coordinator’s endorsement to be credible in the clubhouse, the coordinator has power over the process whatever the chart says. A small data-engineering group that controls the pipeline coaches rely on each morning holds a dependency of the same type as the software platform team. And a leader who introduces a new analytical process should ask, before any meeting, which of those dependencies the process creates, changes or threatens — because people whose leverage a change reduces have a structural reason to resist it, quite apart from what they think of its merits.

**Managing upward through dependence.** Dependence runs in both directions. Your manager depends on you for information, execution, judgment and reputation with others; that mutual dependence is what gives you standing to influence upward. Effective upward influence starts by knowing what your manager is accountable for, what pressures they face, and which of their goals your work advances. The aim is not leverage for its own sake but a relationship in which each side’s dependence on the other is recognized, so that disagreement can be voiced without being read as disloyalty.

apply.title: Executive twist: your power is borrowed

blocks.text: Suppose your influence over a cross-departmental project rests largely on the visible backing of one senior sponsor. That is legitimate power on loan. Sponsors leave, change priorities or lose standing, and borrowed power disappears faster than it arrived. You do not know whether your sponsor will be in place in a year. The executive question is how to convert borrowed power into owned power while you still have it: by building expertise others rely on, by creating dependencies that run through your work rather than through the sponsor, and by earning referent standing with peers. Which of those would you invest in first, and what evidence would tell you it is working?

retain.text: Power is a relation of dependence, perceived by its targets through bases such as legitimacy, reward, expertise and identification. Formal authority is one source among several, and practical power over a change sits with whoever controls something important, with discretion, for which there are few alternatives. Map those dependencies before proposing change, and treat practitioner advice about using power as advice, not evidence.
Without looking back: what are the three conditions that make one actor dependent on another, and which of them can you change most easily in your own work?
Name one person in your organization who sits in the “hidden power holder” cell for a decision you care about. What resource gives them that position?
Why is French and Raven’s typology better treated as a diagnostic vocabulary than as a list of separate levers?

takeaways: Authority is legitimate power granted by position; practical power comes from what others depend on you for.
Dependence rises with a resource’s importance, the holder’s discretion and the scarcity of alternatives.
Power concentrates where critical uncertainty is handled, often below the formal top.
The French and Raven bases are defined by targets’ perceptions and overlap in practice; use them to diagnose, not to calculate.
“Managing with power” advice is a practitioner synthesis; the structural theory beneath it is better supported than its prescriptions.

check.prompt: Which statement best explains the analyst’s influence, using resource dependence logic?

stimulus.text: In a mid-sized insurance company, a junior actuarial analyst maintains the only working model that converts claims data into the reserve estimates the chief financial officer presents to the board each quarter. The model is poorly documented. Two senior managers have tried to have it rebuilt elsewhere; both efforts stalled. The analyst has no direct reports and sits four levels below the CFO, yet her objections to a proposed reporting change have delayed it twice. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: She has referent power because senior managers admire her technical skill.
She controls a resource that is important to the CFO, over which she has discretion, and for which there is currently no alternative source, so the CFO’s side depends on her.
She has legitimate power because the board relies on the reserve estimates.
She has coercive power because she could quit and harm the company.

check.explanation: All three conditions of dependence are present: the reserve estimate is important, the analyst has discretion over how the model is run and changed, and the failed rebuilds show there is no alternative. Power follows dependence regardless of rank. The right executive response is usually to reduce the dependence (documentation, a second person, a rebuild) while respecting the expertise that created it.

optionFeedback.a: Admiration is not described, and referent power rests on identification, not on technical skill. Her leverage comes from the structure of the situation.
optionFeedback.c: Legitimate power rests on accepted rights to direct. Nothing in the vignette gives her that right; the board’s reliance is on the output, not on her authority.
optionFeedback.d: A threat to quit is not mentioned, and coercive power rests on the target’s belief that the agent will impose costs. Her delays come from ordinary objections that others cannot route around.

check.prompt: According to French and Raven, which feature distinguishes coercive power from the other bases in how it must be maintained?

options.text: It depends on the agent’s formal title.
It tends to require surveillance, because compliance lasts only while the agent can observe and punish.
It is limited to the domain in which the agent is knowledgeable.
It operates even when the agent is absent, because the target carries the model with them.

check.explanation: French and Raven noted that coercion produces compliance only under observation and tends to reduce the target’s attraction to the agent. That makes it costly to sustain, which is one reason coercive control scales poorly in large organizations.

optionFeedback.a: Title is the source of legitimate power; coercive power can exist without one (a peer who can block your work can coerce).
optionFeedback.c: Limited range is characteristic of expert power.
optionFeedback.d: Operating in the agent’s absence is characteristic of referent power, the opposite of coercion.

lessons.title: The Organization Behind the Chart: Networks, Brokerage and Social Capital
lessons.summary: Information, advice and trust move through informal networks whose structure — weak ties, bridges and structural holes — predicts who hears what first and whose ideas travel.
objectives: Explain Granovetter’s weak-ties argument and how a randomized test refined it.
Apply Burt’s structural-hole concept to identify brokers and the value and risks of brokerage.
Distinguish advice, trust and communication networks and diagnose common structural problems in an informal network.
Evaluate the causal evidence behind network claims and the cultural limits of brokerage.
lessons.executive: The organization chart shows who reports to whom; informal networks show who asks whom for advice, who trusts whom with bad news, and who talks every day. Granovetter showed that weak ties carry new information across groups; a randomized LinkedIn study confirmed a causal effect but found that moderately weak ties help most. Burt showed that people who bridge disconnected groups — brokers across structural holes — are more likely to have ideas judged valuable. For a leader introducing change, the implication is concrete: find the brokers and the trusted advisers, check whether one person is the only bridge, and remember that much institutional memory lives in relationships rather than documents.

explore.text: Two analysts join a consulting firm’s healthcare practice in the same month with similar credentials. After two years, one has had three of her proposals adopted by clients and partners; the other, whose work reviewers rate as technically stronger, has had none. When the firm’s people team looks more closely, the difference is not in the proposals. The first analyst spent part of her first year on a cross-practice project with the firm’s data science group and kept in loose contact with several people there; she also had lunch, roughly monthly, with a former colleague now at a hospital client. The second analyst worked almost entirely within his own team, which was close-knit, supportive and — he later realized — heard about the same things at the same time he did. (Hypothetical.)

Before reading on: think of the last genuinely new idea or piece of information that changed how you work. From whom did it come? Was that person a close colleague you talk to daily, or someone you see occasionally in another group?

Most people expect important information to come from those closest to them. A substantial body of sociological research says that for *new* information the opposite is often true — and that the structure of your network, not only its size or warmth, shapes what you know, when you know it, and whether others will hear your ideas.

blocks.text: A social network is a set of **nodes** (people, teams or organizations) and **ties** (relationships between them). Ties can be strong — frequent, emotionally close, reciprocal — or weak, such as acquaintances. A network’s **density** is the share of possible ties that exist; in a dense cluster nearly everyone knows everyone else. A **bridge** is a tie that provides the only path between two parts of a network. **Centrality** measures describe how important a node’s position is: degree centrality counts direct ties, while betweenness centrality captures how often a node lies on the shortest paths between others — a rough measure of brokerage. **Social capital** is the advantage a person or group gains from the structure and content of its relationships.

understand.text: The strength of weak ties

Mark Granovetter’s 1973 paper starts from a simple observation. If A is strongly tied to both B and C, then B and C are likely to know each other too, because people spend time with their close friends’ close friends. Strong ties therefore cluster into dense groups in which information circulates quickly and becomes redundant. The ties that connect one cluster to another — the bridges — are almost always weak ties, because a strong tie would have pulled the two clusters together. It follows that weak ties carry information that is new to the receiving group. Granovetter supported the argument with data on how professional, technical and managerial workers had found their jobs: among those who found jobs through personal contacts, the contacts were more often people they saw occasionally or rarely than people they saw often.

Ronald Burt shifted attention from the strength of ties to the gaps between groups. A **structural hole** is the absence of a tie between two groups that each hold different information. A person whose network spans the hole — a **broker** — sees opinions and practices from both sides earlier than people inside either group, and can combine them. In a study of supply-chain managers at a large American electronics company, Burt found that managers whose networks spanned structural holes were more likely to express ideas, less likely to have them dismissed, and more likely to have them judged valuable by senior managers; brokerage was also associated with compensation, positive evaluations and promotion. Burt contrasts this brokerage advantage with the advantages of **closure** — dense networks in which everyone knows everyone, which make trust and enforcement of norms easier.

understand.text: Three informal networks, not one

David Krackhardt and Jeffrey Hanson, writing for managers, argued that the formal chart is a poor guide to how work gets done, and that informal networks can be mapped with a few survey questions. They distinguished three networks that rarely coincide. The **advice network** shows who people depend on to solve problems and get technical information. The **trust network** shows who shares sensitive political information and who backs whom in a crisis. The **communication network** shows who talks about work-related matters on a regular basis. A person can be central in the advice network and peripheral in the trust network, which is exactly the profile of a technically respected expert whose proposals for change are not believed. They also described recurring structural patterns, such as a single person who is the only link between otherwise separate groups.

understand.caption: Advice centrality versus trust centrality: four profiles for change agents
cells: **Outsider.** Neither consulted nor confided in; rarely decisive, sometimes a fresh view.
**Confidant.** Trusted with bad news but not consulted on technical matters; crucial for reading resistance and legitimacy.
**Respected technician.** Asked how, not whether. Strong on the content of a change, weak at making it credible.
**Linchpin.** Both consulted and trusted. Win this person and many follow; lose them and the change stalls.
understand.note: Teaching device built on Krackhardt and Hanson’s distinction between advice and trust networks.

understand.text: Networks also hold **institutional memory**. Much of what an organization knows — why a policy exists, which past experiment failed and why, who promised what to whom — is not written down. It lives in relationships and is retrieved by knowing whom to ask. When a long-tenured broker leaves, the organization loses not only a person but the paths along which that knowledge traveled. Trust behaves similarly: it accumulates through repeated interaction along particular ties, and it is spent quickly when someone uses a relationship purely instrumentally.

challenge.text: How much of the network advantage is causal? Granovetter’s original evidence and Burt’s firm data are observational. People who are talented, outgoing or ambitious may build bridging networks *and* do well for the same underlying reasons, and good ideas may attract contacts rather than the reverse. A large test addressed this for weak ties. Using randomized variation in LinkedIn’s “People You May Know” recommendations across more than 20 million members, Karthik Rajkumar, Sinan Aral and colleagues found causal evidence that weak ties matter for job mobility — but with an inverted-U shape: moderately weak ties were most helpful, and the weakest ties were not. Weak ties also mattered more in more digital industries. The classic claim survived a causal test, in a more precise and less sloganlike form. No comparable randomized test exists for Burt’s brokerage claims inside organizations.

Brokerage may not travel equally well across cultures or settings. In a workplace that prizes loyalty to a close group, a person seen moving information between groups for personal advantage may lose more in trust than they gain in information. A plausible hypothesis, which you should test against your own experience rather than accept, is that brokerage pays best where it is seen as connecting people for a shared purpose and worst where it is seen as playing groups against each other. Leaders who work across national or linguistic boundaries — for example between U.S. and Latin American operations — often occupy precisely this structural position, and how they are read may depend on whether they are seen as translators for both sides or gatekeepers for one.

Finally, network advice can be misused. Mapping who confides in whom is useful and also intrusive. A network survey that people later learn was used to identify “blockers” will poison trust in the next survey and in the leader who commissioned it. Use network diagnostics transparently, with a clear purpose, aggregated where possible, and never to target individuals for having the wrong friends.

challenge.title: Methodological note: the network data problem

blocks.text: Network research faces problems that ordinary survey research does not. **Boundary specification**: deciding who counts as part of the network changes every measure of centrality. **Informant accuracy**: people are reasonably good at reporting typical patterns of interaction but poor at recalling specific interactions, and they systematically misperceive ties among others. **Missing data**: a single non-respondent removes all of that person’s ties, which can distort brokerage measures dramatically. **Endogeneity**: networks are not randomly assigned, and people with similar traits tend to connect (homophily), so similarities among connected people may reflect selection rather than influence. Distinguishing influence from homophily in observational network data is notoriously hard; that is why the platform experiment above, which randomized the formation of ties, is so valuable.

For a practitioner this means two things. First, treat any network map as a hypothesis about the organization, not a photograph of it. Second, prefer behavioral traces (who actually co-authored, co-attended, emailed) to recalled ties when the stakes are high — while recognizing that traces carry their own privacy obligations.

apply.text: Consider three hypothetical brokers. In a state public-health department, an epidemiologist who used to work in the emergency medical services agency is the only person both agencies call when overdose data look strange; every interagency question passes through her, and when she takes leave, joint work stops. In a technology company, a product manager who rotates among engineering, sales and legal hears early that a large customer’s procurement rules are changing, and proposes a feature redesign weeks before anyone else sees the issue. In a hospital, a nurse informaticist who sits between the clinical units and the IT department is trusted by nurses because she worked nights for a decade; IT treats her as a translator, and the units treat her as one of their own.

Each example shows a different managerial task. The epidemiologist is a bow tie: the organization is fragile, and the fix is to add redundant ties and record what she knows. The product manager shows brokerage producing a valuable idea early, which leaders should protect and reward. The nurse informaticist is a linchpin in both advice and trust networks; any change in clinical technology should involve her early, but leaders should avoid overloading her or making her responsible for selling decisions she did not help shape.

In player development the same structures are easy to recognize. A bilingual coordinator who moves between an international academy and domestic affiliates bridges a structural hole that language and geography create. That position is valuable — early warning about players’ adjustment, ideas from one environment that solve problems in the other — and fragile, because the organization may have only one such bridge. A leader introducing a new analytical or operational process should ask who sits in the advice network for coaches (often a respected veteran instructor), who sits in the trust network (often someone with long tenure and no evaluative role), and whether the process will travel through those people or around them. Processes routed around trusted brokers tend to arrive without credibility.

A practical routine for any change: list the groups the change touches; for each pair of groups, name who connects them; mark any pair connected by only one person; and for each group, name who is most consulted and who is most trusted. That routine is the core of the Influence Map exercise this week.

retain.text: Informal networks carry information, advice and trust along paths the chart does not show. Weak ties and brokerage across structural holes bring new information and good ideas, though the causal evidence is strongest for weak ties and shows that moderately weak ties help most. check.prompt: What is the most accurate conclusion from the study described?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract. Researchers surveyed 240 engineers at one firm about whom they discussed work with, computed each engineer’s brokerage score, and linked it to the number of patents filed over the next two years. Engineers in the top quartile of brokerage filed about twice as many patents as those in the bottom quartile. The authors conclude: “Spanning structural holes causes innovation; firms should rotate engineers across teams.”

options.text: The conclusion is justified because brokerage was measured before patenting.

The data show an association consistent with brokerage theory, but able or ambitious engineers may both build bridging networks and patent more; the causal claim and the rotation policy go beyond the evidence.
The study shows that brokerage has no effect, because patents measure quantity, not quality.
The study is invalid because network data cannot be collected by survey.

check.explanation: Measuring brokerage first establishes timing but not causation: a third factor (ability, ambition, role) could drive both brokerage and patenting. The finding is consistent with Burt’s theory, which is itself observational. A causal claim would need variation in network position that is unrelated to engineers’ traits — for example randomized rotation.

optionFeedback.a: Temporal order is necessary for causation but not sufficient; confounding by ability or role remains.
optionFeedback.c: The quantity measure is a limitation, but it does not show the absence of an effect.
optionFeedback.d: Surveys are a standard, if imperfect, way to collect network data; their limits (recall, missing data) do not make a study invalid.

Her proposals are technically weak.

optionFeedback.c: Legitimate power helps but is not required; many changes are driven by people without formal authority.

lessons.title: Coalitions, Legitimacy and the Politics of Change
lessons.summary: Organizations are negotiated settlements among coalitions embedded in fields that reward legitimacy; change succeeds when it renegotiates the settlement and earns legitimacy without being captured by it.
objectives: Explain the behavioral theory of the firm’s view of organizations as political coalitions and its implications for change.
Distinguish coercive, mimetic and normative isomorphism and identify legitimacy-driven adoption.
Analyze co-optation as a coalition strategy, including its cost in mission drift.
Interpret resistance to change as information about threatened bargains rather than as irrationality.
lessons.executive: Organizations are not single actors with one goal. They are coalitions whose goals are bargained, held together by side payments and slack, and attended to one at a time. A change proposal reopens those bargains, so resistance is often a rational defense of a settlement, not a failure of understanding. Organizations also live in fields that reward looking legitimate: they copy peers under uncertainty, follow professional norms and comply with those they depend on. Leaders can borrow legitimacy and can co-opt opponents by giving them a share of control — but, as Selznick showed, co-optation can bend the mission toward the co-opted. Plan the coalition, the legitimacy and the price.

explore.text: A state government announces that three agencies — workforce training, vocational rehabilitation and adult education — will be consolidated into a single department to give residents “one front door”. Eighteen months later the new department exists on paper. Its website has one logo. But the three former agencies still run separate intake systems, report to separate legislative committees, draw on separate federal funding streams with separate rules, and hold separate staff meetings. The merged department’s first director, who championed the idea, has left. Asked what happened, a long-serving deputy says simply: “Nobody asked the people who had to give something up.” (Hypothetical.)

Before reading on: in a reorganization like this, list who gains and who loses — in budget, autonomy, status, workload or relationships with funders. Which losers had the ability to slow the change without ever openly opposing it?

The story is common enough that it is tempting to file it under “bureaucracy”. Organizational sociology offers something sharper: two theories that explain why such changes stall, and one classic study that explains the hidden price of the most common remedy.

understand.title: Prerequisite: what sociologists mean by an “institution”

blocks.text: In everyday speech an institution is a large organization. In organizational sociology the word means something closer to a **settled way of doing things** that people take for granted — a rule, norm, role or practice that persists because it is seen as legitimate or simply as “how it is done”, not only because it is efficient. Professional credentials, budget cycles, the annual performance review and the idea that a hospital must have a quality department are all institutions in this sense. An **organizational field** is the set of organizations that recognize one another as engaged in a common activity — all public-health departments, all large law firms, all clubs in a league — together with their regulators, suppliers and professional bodies.

understand.text: The organization as a political coalition

Richard Cyert and James March, an economist and a political scientist, challenged the economic picture of the firm as a single profit-maximizing decision maker. In *A Behavioral Theory of the Firm* they described the organization as a coalition of individuals and groups — managers, workers, owners, specialists — whose goals differ. The organization’s goals are the product of bargaining among coalition members. Because the bargaining is never complete, conflict is never fully resolved; it is held in check by attending to different goals at different times, by **side payments** (budget, status, autonomy, policy commitments) that keep members in the coalition, and by **organizational slack**, the surplus resources that let the organization pay several members at once. Organizations, in this view, aim for satisfactory rather than optimal outcomes and search for new solutions mainly when performance falls below aspiration.

Later organizational theorists began to speak of the **dominant coalition**: the subset of members whose agreement actually determines major decisions. The concept is useful precisely because it is not the same as the top of the chart. A change agent’s first strategic question is therefore not “who is in charge?” but “what is the current settlement, who is party to it, and what does each party receive for staying in?”

understand.caption: Why change proposals meet resistance: the coalition view

steps.label: Settlement
steps.text: Coalition members hold side payments: budget, autonomy, status, workload, relationships.

steps.label: Proposal
steps.text: A change reallocates some of those payments, often implicitly.

steps.label: Threat
steps.text: Members who lose — or fear losing — see the bargain reopened.

steps.label: Resistance
steps.text: Open objection, delay, minimal compliance, appeals to outside allies.

steps.label: Renegotiation
steps.text: New side payments, co-optation, a new coalition, or borrowed legitimacy.

steps.label: New settlement
steps.text: Stable only if enough members, with enough power, prefer it to the old one.

understand.text: Institutional isomorphism and legitimacy

Paul DiMaggio and Walter Powell asked a different question: why are organizations in the same field so similar? Their answer was that, once a field is established, organizations converge less because similarity is efficient than because of **institutional isomorphism**. **Coercive** isomorphism arises from pressure by organizations they depend on and by the state — funders’ reporting rules, regulators’ mandates. **Mimetic** isomorphism arises under uncertainty: when goals are ambiguous or technologies poorly understood, organizations copy peers that look successful. **Normative** isomorphism arises from professionalization: people trained in the same programs and active in the same associations bring the same templates with them. Conforming to these pressures confers **legitimacy** — the perception that the organization is appropriate and proper — which in turn helps secure resources and support.

understand.text: Co-optation and its price

Philip Selznick’s study of the Tennessee Valley Authority, published in 1949, examined a federal agency committed to “grass-roots” administration that worked through established local institutions and elites. Selznick developed the concept of **co-optation**: absorbing new elements into an organization’s leadership or policy-making structure to avert threats to its stability or existence. He distinguished formal co-optation, which shares the symbols of participation, from informal co-optation, which shares real power with influential outside interests. His central and still uncomfortable finding was that co-optation has a price. The interests brought inside acquire leverage over the organization’s actual commitments, so that the support an agency buys can quietly redirect its programs away from its stated goals.

challenge.text: Each theory has blind spots. The coalition view can make every organizational decision look like a bargain among self-interested parties, which underestimates genuine shared commitment to a mission; many professionals accept losses of budget or status because they believe a change is right. Institutional theory, in its strong form, predicts more sameness and less agency than we observe: some organizations deliberately break with their field and succeed, and individual leaders sometimes create new institutions rather than merely conforming. And Selznick’s account is one historical case, richly interpreted, not a general law about how often co-optation backfires.

**Resistance reconsidered.** Popular change-management writing often treats resistance as an emotional reaction to be overcome. The coalition view suggests a more useful default: resistance is frequently a rational response by people whose side payments a proposal threatens, and it often carries information the change agent lacks — about workload that was invisible from above, commitments to outside partners, or past attempts that failed for reasons no one recorded. Some resistance is self-interested and some is principled; treating all of it as irrational wastes the information in the second kind and inflames the first.

A related caution concerns legitimacy itself. When adoption is driven by legitimacy rather than results, organizations can adopt the visible form of a practice — the department, the dashboard, the title — while the underlying work continues unchanged. DiMaggio and Powell’s framework predicts exactly this risk under mimetic and coercive pressure. A leader who wants real change must therefore distinguish being *seen* to adopt a practice from adopting it, and should be wary of claiming success on the first.

challenge.title: Methodological note: how would you know a practice was adopted for legitimacy?

blocks.text: Institutional explanations are hard to test because the same observable pattern — a practice spreading through a field — is predicted by rival explanations. Organizations might copy a practice because it is legitimate, or because they rationally learned from peers that it works. Researchers who study diffusion therefore look for distinguishing signatures. Legitimacy-driven adoption predicts that adoption will depend on peers’ adoption and visibility more than on evidence of performance, that late adopters will adopt in more ceremonial forms, and that adopters will vary little in how deeply they implement. Efficiency-driven adoption predicts that adoption will track expected benefit and that late adopters, having learned from early ones, will implement more deeply.

Studies often model the timing of adoption across many organizations (event-history analysis) and test which predictors matter. The difficulty is that “peers adopted it” is also a rational signal. For an executive, the usable lesson is diagnostic: when someone argues that your organization must adopt a practice “because everyone has one”, ask what evidence exists that it changes outcomes, and design your version so that its results can be checked rather than merely displayed.

apply.text: Consider three hypothetical change agents. A hospital chief quality officer wants every unit to use a new handoff protocol. The surgical department chair, whose surgeons dislike it, also chairs the medical staff committee that credentials physicians. The officer can co-opt the chair by asking him to lead the protocol’s adaptation for surgery — gaining his support at the price of letting surgery shape its own version. In a financial firm, a new chief risk officer seeks to tighten limits on a profitable trading desk; the desk head is part of the dominant coalition because the desk funds bonuses across the firm. In a city government, a performance-management director builds legitimacy for a new data program by adopting the reporting format used by peer cities a national association promotes, making the program look familiar to council members.

In each case, map three things. **The settlement**: who receives what now — and what would the change take away? **The legitimacy**: which external audiences (regulators, professions, peers, the public) will judge the change, and which templates will make it look proper? **The price**: if you co-opt an opponent or borrow a template, what control over the change do you give away, and where is your line? A co-optation strategy is sound when the co-opted party’s influence improves the design or is confined to matters you can concede. It is dangerous when it hands them control of the core purpose.

Sports organizations are coalitions too. A new player-development process may shift budget toward technology, alter which staff members’ judgment carries weight in decisions about players, and change who is consulted before a promotion. Coaches, scouts, analysts, medical staff and senior executives each hold a side payment in the current arrangement, often in the form of professional respect and voice. Legitimacy pressures are also strong: in a league where peer organizations are seen adopting a practice, a club may be pressed to adopt it whether or not it fits — mimetic isomorphism. A leader introducing a process should be able to say which coalition members gain and lose, what each would accept, which professional norms make the process feel legitimate to coaches, and what the leader will not trade away to win support.

apply.title: Executive twist: the coalition you inherit

blocks.text: You take over a department in the middle of a change initiative your predecessor launched. Several senior staff members were promised roles in the new structure; you do not know exactly what was promised, and the documentation is thin. Two of them are now its loudest advocates, and one is quietly slowing it down. Honoring every promise would lock in a design you doubt. Breaking them would signal that commitments in this organization are worthless, which damages trust far beyond this project. With incomplete information, what would you find out first, from whom, and how would you decide which commitments the organization must keep even if you would not have made them?

retain.text: Organizations are coalitions held together by bargained side payments, so change reopens settlements and invites resistance that is often rational. Fields reward legitimacy through coercive, mimetic and normative pressure, which can produce ceremonial adoption. Co-optation buys support by sharing control, and the price can be the mission itself.

Give one example each of coercive, mimetic and normative isomorphism from a field you know.

Resistance often defends a threatened bargain and carries information the change agent lacks.
Coercive, mimetic and normative isomorphism push organizations to adopt practices for legitimacy, sometimes only ceremonially.
Co-optation gains support by sharing control; set in advance what you will not concede.

check.prompt: You lead a statewide initiative to standardize child-welfare case-review practices across counties. The association of county directors opposes it. Which co-optation design best captures support while limiting Selznick’s risk of mission drift?

lessons.title: Influence Without Authority: Tactics, Issue Selling and the Ethics of Persuasion
lessons.summary: How you try to influence — upward, sideways or down — predicts whether people commit, comply or resist, and persuasion research is useful only when read with its replication record and an ethical line.
objectives: Compare influence tactics by the commitment they tend to produce and by direction (boss, peers, subordinates).
Apply Dutton and Ashford’s issue-selling framework to plan upward influence.
Evaluate compliance principles in light of the replication evidence.
Apply explicit tests to distinguish legitimate persuasion from manipulation.
lessons.executive: When you lack authority over the people you need, the tactic you choose matters. In field research, rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation were most associated with genuine commitment; pressure, appeals to rules and coalition tactics with the least. Some tactics that work with peers and staff — ingratiation, exchange — did not work upward. To get senior leaders to attend to an issue, package it (framing, linking it to their goals) and manage the process (timing, channels, allies), knowing that sellers risk their image. Compliance principles such as reciprocity and social proof are real, but many specific effects are smaller than early studies suggested. Use influence you would be comfortable having disclosed.

explore.text: A product manager at a software company needs three things she does not control: two weeks of a security engineer’s time from another team, a change to the sales team’s demonstration script, and her vice president’s willingness to raise a pricing problem with the chief executive. She has no authority over any of these people. A colleague advises her to “escalate early, copy the VP on everything, and make it clear the CEO wants this.” Another tells her to “figure out what each of them needs and start there.” (Hypothetical.)

Before reading on: for each of the three requests, which approach would you choose — a reasoned case, an appeal to shared purpose, asking for their input, a trade, an appeal to rules or senior backing, or persistent pressure? Write your choice and why.

Most executive work is influence without authority: over peers who have their own priorities, over bosses who set agendas, over partners outside the organization. This lesson covers what the evidence says about influence tactics, how to bring an issue to senior attention, what persuasion research does and does not support, and where persuasion becomes manipulation.

blocks.text: Influence researchers distinguish three outcomes. **Commitment** means the target agrees inwardly and works to make the request succeed, including in ways no one can monitor. **Compliance** means the target does what was asked, often minimally, without believing in it. **Resistance** means the target refuses, delays, argues or complies in form only. For most changes that matter — a new process, a different way of evaluating people — compliance is not enough, because the work depends on effort and judgment that cannot be supervised. That is why the question is not only “will they do it?” but “will they want it to work?”

understand.text: Influence tactics and their consequences

Gary Yukl and J. Bruce Tracey studied the influence tactics managers used with subordinates, peers and bosses, and asked the targets how committed they became. Rational persuasion (logical arguments and evidence), inspirational appeals (linking a request to the target’s values and ideals) and consultation (inviting the target to help plan or shape the request) were the tactics most associated with commitment. Pressure (demands, threats, persistent checking), legitimating tactics (appeals to rules, authority or precedent) and coalition tactics (enlisting others to push the target) were least effective. Ingratiation and exchange — creating goodwill, or offering something in return — were moderately effective with subordinates and peers but not with superiors.

Requires knowing what the target cares about
Inviting the target to shape the plan

understand.text: Notice that coalition tactics score poorly as a *tactic* aimed at a target, even though building a coalition is essential to change (Lesson 3). The difference is between assembling support for a proposal, which strengthens its legitimacy, and using allies to pressure a particular person, which the target experiences as being outnumbered. The first is coalition-building; the second is a pressure tactic in another form.
Selling issues upward

Jane Dutton and Susan Ashford argued that middle managers shape what top management attends to by **selling issues** — drawing attention to trends, problems and opportunities and framing them. They built their framework from three perspectives: issue selling as upward influence, as a claiming behavior (asserting that something deserves attention), and as impression management, because the seller’s image is at stake. Whether a manager tries to sell an issue depends on the perceived chance of success and on image risk; whether the attempt works depends on **packaging** — how the issue is framed and whether it is bundled with other concerns leaders already hold — and on **process**: timing, the formality of the channel, and whether others are involved.

steps.label: Read the context
steps.text: What is leadership already worried about? What is the cost of raising this now?

steps.label: Frame
steps.text: Link the issue to goals leaders own; state it as an opportunity or a threat deliberately.

steps.label: Bundle
steps.text: Connect it to issues already on the agenda, or separate it if bundling would bury it.

steps.label: Choose the channel
steps.text: Informal first conversation or formal proposal; one-on-one or in a forum.

steps.label: Involve others
steps.text: Who should co-sponsor, and who must not be surprised?

steps.label: Time it
steps.text: Budget cycles, crises, leadership transitions open and close windows.

understand.text: Compliance principles

Robert Cialdini’s research program identified principles through which people are moved to comply: **reciprocity** (we feel obliged to return favors and concessions), **commitment and consistency** (we act in line with what we have already said or done), **social proof** (we look to what similar others do), **liking**, **authority** and **scarcity**. In a review with Noah Goldstein, Cialdini organized compliance and conformity around three goals they serve — being accurate, affiliating with others, and maintaining a positive self-concept — and emphasized that much influence works subtly, outside awareness. They also stressed the role of norms: descriptive norms (what people do) and injunctive norms (what people approve of).

challenge.text: How much of the compliance literature replicates? The picture is mixed and you should hold it that way. Some classic findings have held up well: in 2021 Oliver Genschow and colleagues directly replicated the 1975 door-in-the-face study by Cialdini and colleagues — in which a refused large request increases compliance with a smaller one — on a German university campus with 410 people, finding compliance rates similar to the original and results consistent with the reciprocity explanation. The authors themselves caution that this is one replication of one finding. Other effects in the broader social-influence literature have proved smaller or less consistent than early studies suggested, and the 2004 review predates the replication crisis that led psychologists to re-examine small-sample results. A reasonable reading is that the principles name real mechanisms, while the size of any specific technique’s effect — especially between colleagues who will work together again — is uncertain.

There is also a mismatch of settings. Most compliance experiments involve one-off requests between strangers. Organizational influence happens in repeated relationships where people remember how they were treated. A technique that wins a single request but feels manipulative once noticed can cost more in the next ten interactions than it gained in the first. This is one reason the tactics associated with commitment in field studies — reasons, purpose, consultation — are the ones that respect the target’s judgment.

Tactic effectiveness probably varies across cultures and relationships. In workplaces where personal relationships carry more of the weight of cooperation — which leaders with experience across U.S. and Latin American organizations often describe — personal appeals and relationship-based exchange may be expected and legitimate rather than suspect, and a purely “rational” approach may read as cold. Treat this as a hypothesis to check against local norms, not as a stereotype to apply: individuals vary far more than national averages suggest.

challenge.title: Methodological note: why influence-tactic studies are hard to interpret

blocks.text: Most evidence on influence tactics comes from questionnaires in which agents or targets describe tactics and outcomes. Three problems follow. **Common-method bias**: when the same person reports both the tactic and their own commitment, a general positive or negative impression of the agent can drive both answers. **Reverse causation and selection**: agents choose tactics in light of expected resistance. A manager who expects strong opposition is more likely to use pressure, so pressure may be associated with resistance partly because it is used where resistance was already likely. **Recall and labeling**: targets may label a request they agreed with as “rational persuasion” and one they resented as “pressure”.

Studies that collect reports from targets rather than agents, as Yukl and Tracey did, reduce some of these problems but not all. Experiments can randomize tactics but usually lose the realism of ongoing work relationships. The pattern across methods is consistent enough to act on, but the precise ranking of tactics is less certain than a summary table makes it look.

challenge.text: Influence is not ethically neutral, and executives are rarely taught where the lines are. Three practical tests help. **The disclosure test**: would the approach still work, and would you still be comfortable, if the target knew exactly what you were doing and why? Reasons and consultation pass easily; manufactured scarcity or a staged concession does not. **The interest test**: does the influence attempt help the target decide in light of their own interests and values, or does it bypass their judgment? **The reversibility test**: would you accept being influenced this way by someone with the opposite goal?

challenge.caption: Persuasion and manipulation: two questions
cells: **Manipulation.** Exploiting a bias to secure agreement against the target’s interest. Off limits.
**Hard bargaining.** Honest arguments pursued for your side only. Legitimate but costly to trust if repeated.
**Paternalistic nudge.** Steering someone toward what you judge good for them without their awareness. Contested; requires transparency and a defensible reason.
**Persuasion.** Honest reasons and evidence offered for a choice that serves the target too. The default.
challenge.note: Teaching device. The ethical lines in your engagement plan should state which cells you will not enter.

apply.text: Return to the product manager. For the security engineer’s time, consultation and exchange are natural: ask the engineer’s manager what their team needs this quarter and whether a trade of time or credit would help. For the sales script, rational persuasion with evidence from lost deals, plus consultation with the sales lead on wording, is likely to produce commitment; escalation “because the CEO wants it” is a legitimating tactic that may produce a script change and a quietly unconvinced sales team. For the pricing problem, issue selling applies: frame it in terms of revenue goals the vice president owns, choose a private first conversation rather than a meeting where the VP could be surprised, and offer to co-present rather than ask the VP to carry the risk alone.

The same logic travels. A junior associate in a law firm who wants partners to adopt a new contract-review tool will fare better framing it as a response to a client complaint the partners already worry about than as a technology upgrade. A staff officer recommending a change to a commander can use rational persuasion while making clear that the decision remains the commander’s, preserving the legitimacy of the chain of command. A nurse who wants hospital leaders to act on a staffing risk must weigh the image risk Dutton and Ashford described: being seen as a complainer may cost more than the issue gains, unless it is framed around patient safety goals leaders have publicly committed to.

In a professional baseball organization, a leader introducing a new analytical process will usually need to influence upward (a senior executive who must fund it), sideways (peer department heads whose staff must use it) and down (coaches and analysts who will do the work). The evidence suggests leading with reasons and with the purpose the process serves for players, consulting coaches on how it fits their routines, and offering exchange where peers bear costs — while avoiding the tempting shortcut of announcing that “the front office has decided”, a legitimating tactic that tends to win compliance without commitment. Implementing an improvement without undermining existing relationships means treating those relationships as assets the change must protect, not as obstacles to route around.

apply.title: Executive twist: when you are the target

blocks.text: As you gain authority, you become the target of influence far more often than the agent. Subordinates frame issues to fit what they think you want; peers bundle their requests with your priorities; vendors manufacture scarcity. You will rarely see the full picture, and some of the people influencing you are right. What routines — asking for the strongest counterargument, delaying decisions made under artificial deadlines, seeking out the person who has not spoken — would you adopt so that you can be persuaded by good reasons without being steered by technique?

retain.text: Reasons, purpose and consultation tend to produce commitment; pressure, appeals to rules and ganging up tend to produce compliance or resistance, and some tactics that work with peers fail upward. Issue selling depends on packaging and process, and carries image risk. Compliance principles are real mechanisms with uncertain effect sizes, and influence should pass the disclosure test.

Presenting the evidence for the project and inviting the peer to help design how their staff would be involved.
Reminding the peer that the organization’s policy requires cross-departmental cooperation.

check.explanation: Combining rational persuasion with consultation uses the two tactics most associated with commitment and gives the peer ownership of the part of the plan that affects their staff.

check.prompt: What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

stimulus.text: “A replication in Germany confirmed the door-in-the-face effect almost fifty years after the original. That proves Cialdini’s principles are settled science, so we should train our managers to use the technique in internal budget negotiations.”

options.text: The replication was conducted in a different country, so it cannot be relevant.

One successful replication of one technique, with strangers making one-off requests, does not establish all the principles or the size of the effect in repeated relationships among colleagues — and the ethical question is left unaddressed.
The original study was too old to be worth replicating.
Door-in-the-face is a pressure tactic and therefore never works.

check.explanation: The argument overgeneralizes from one technique to all principles and from strangers to colleagues. The replication supports the reciprocity mechanism but says nothing about effects in ongoing relationships, where a staged concession that is noticed can damage trust; it also skips the disclosure test.

optionFeedback.a: Replication in a new country strengthens confidence in generality; it is not a flaw.
optionFeedback.c: Age is not a reason to dismiss a finding; the replication was valuable precisely because older findings are rarely retested.
optionFeedback.d: Door-in-the-face is a reciprocity-based technique, and the replication shows it can work; the issue is overgeneralization, not that it never works.

The principle that A’s power over B equals B’s dependence on A, which grows with the importance of what A controls, A’s discretion over it, and B’s lack of alternatives.

A relationship of low frequency or intimacy, such as an acquaintance; per Granovetter, the kind of tie that usually bridges groups and carries new information.

The subset of organizational members whose agreement actually determines major decisions; not necessarily the top of the formal chart.
