exercise.title: Influence Map

intro.text: You will map the people who will decide whether a fictional hospital system adopts a change. Read each profile and the known ties. For every person, rate **power** over this specific change (1–5), **interest** in it (1–5) and current **stance** (−2 strongly opposed to +2 strongly supportive). The tool will plot a power/interest grid, total supporting and opposing power, flag powerful neutrals and brokers tied to both camps, and suggest an engagement approach for each quadrant. When you submit, the case author’s read appears beside yours.

As you rate, use the week’s tools rather than intuition alone. For power, ask what each person controls that the change depends on — importance, discretion, alternatives (Lesson 1) — not only their title. For brokers and trusted figures, use the ties (Lesson 2). For stance, ask what each person’s side payment is in the current arrangement and what the change would take away (Lesson 3).

Notice where your ratings differ most from the author’s. Differences are not errors to be corrected; they are the places where your assumptions about the organization are doing the most work, and where you would most need more information in a real setting.

brief.text: **Tessaly Valley Health** (fictional) runs three community hospitals. Its leadership wants to adopt a **nurse-activated rapid response protocol**: an electronic deterioration score is computed for every adult inpatient, and any bedside nurse who sees a high score or is worried about a patient may summon the rapid response team directly, without first reaching the attending physician. Today nurses must page the physician, who decides whether to call the team. The chief medical officer is sponsoring the change after two internal reviews found delays in escalating care for deteriorating patients.

The change redistributes several things at once: the right to decide when to escalate (from physicians toward nurses), workload (toward the rapid response team, run by critical care), budget (more rapid response staffing), and exposure (who is accountable when a call is late or unnecessary). The organization is unionized for nurses. An accreditation survey is expected within eighteen months. All people, the organization and the details are fictional.

config.goal: Within twelve months, have all three Tessaly Valley hospitals using the nurse-activated rapid response protocol in every adult inpatient unit, with nurses actually activating it when warranted.

stakeholders.name: Dr. Miriam Achterberg
stakeholders.title: Chief Medical Officer (system)
stakeholders.profile: Sponsor of the change. Formally oversees physician quality across the three hospitals. Respected but seen by some hospitalists as “administration now”. Has told the board the protocol will be in place within a year.

key.why: Legitimate power and budget influence, and she has publicly committed — which raises her interest but also her exposure if the rollout falters. Her support is necessary and not sufficient: physicians on the units do not depend on her day to day.

stakeholders.name: Rosalind Tate
stakeholders.title: Chief Nursing Officer (system)
stakeholders.profile: Supports earlier escalation in principle. Worried about nurse workload, documentation burden and whether nurses will be blamed for “unnecessary” calls. Has a close working relationship with the union steward.

key.why: Controls nursing practice standards and staffing; nothing reaches the bedside without her. Supportive but conditional — her conditions (no blame, manageable documentation) are reasonable design inputs and make her a natural co-owner.

stakeholders.name: Dr. Owen Prakash
stakeholders.title: Chair of Hospital Medicine
stakeholders.profile: Leads the hospitalist group that attends most inpatients. Has said in a meeting that bypassing the physician “fragments care” and that nurses will call for things he could handle. His group’s satisfaction scores matter to retention, which the CFO watches closely.

key.why: Hospitalists lose decision rights and gain potential interruptions; a classic threatened side payment. His group can slow adoption informally by signalling disapproval when nurses activate. Treat his objections as information (fragmentation is a real risk) and offer bounded influence — for example, designing the physician notification step.

stakeholders.name: Lucía Ferreira
stakeholders.title: Night-shift charge nurse, medical-surgical unit, North hospital
stakeholders.profile: Twenty years on the unit. Colleagues across all three hospitals ask her for advice; she trains most new night nurses. Skeptical of past “alarm” projects that produced false alerts. Has not said what she thinks of this one.

key.why: A hidden power holder: no title, but she controls the credibility of the protocol among bedside nurses (important, at her discretion, few alternatives). Central in both advice and trust networks. Her neutrality is the single most important open question on the map.

stakeholders.name: Gideon Marsh
stakeholders.title: Director of Critical Care; runs the rapid response team
stakeholders.profile: His team will absorb the extra calls. He supports early escalation clinically but has warned that without added staff the team will be pulled away from the intensive care unit at dangerous moments.

key.why: Mild opposition grounded in a legitimate capacity problem. His concern is resolvable with resources and call-volume monitoring; if resolved, he could become a credible clinical champion.

stakeholders.name: Priya Nandakumar
stakeholders.title: Nurse informaticist
stakeholders.profile: Former intensive care nurse who now configures the electronic record. Trusted by nurses and by IT; she is the person both sides call when the record does something strange. Thinks the score is promising but the alert design needs work.

key.why: Low formal power but a broker between IT and the units, tied to supporters and to the skeptical charge nurse. Her design concerns are valuable; involving her improves the change and its credibility. Avoid overloading her as the only bridge.

stakeholders.name: Calvin Brooks
stakeholders.title: Chief Financial Officer
stakeholders.profile: Has not engaged. Will be asked to fund additional rapid response staffing. Tracks physician retention costs.

key.why: A high-power neutral with low interest — keep satisfied and give a clear, bounded cost case. He becomes an opponent if the request arrives as a surprise or if hospitalist retention appears at risk.

stakeholders.name: Dana Whitfield
stakeholders.title: Union steward, registered nurses
stakeholders.profile: Represents nurses at the North and Central hospitals. Will ask whether nurses who activate the team, or fail to, face discipline, and whether documentation adds unpaid work.

key.why: Power from the collective agreement and from nurses’ trust. Her opposition is conditional on workload and blame; a written no-blame activation policy agreed with nursing leadership could move her to neutral or support.

stakeholders.name: Dr. Hana Okoro
stakeholders.title: Chief Quality and Patient Safety Officer
stakeholders.profile: Led one of the two reviews that found escalation delays. Wants the protocol in place before the accreditation survey.

key.why: Strong supporter who brings legitimacy (patient safety evidence, accreditation expectations). Risk: if she frames the change mainly as “the surveyors expect it”, it may be adopted ceremonially.

stakeholders.name: Dr. Ezra Lindqvist
stakeholders.title: Senior hospitalist, South hospital
stakeholders.profile: Long-tenured, a respected teacher of residents and nurses. Close to Dr. Prakash but also eats lunch with night-shift nurses. Once told a colleague that “half our codes are late calls”.

key.why: A broker tied to both the opposing hospitalist leadership and the nursing network. His private view suggests openness. As an early, consulted adopter on his unit he could provide physician-side social proof that the chair cannot easily dismiss.

config.rules: Practitioner heuristic: the power/interest grid (Mendelow-style stakeholder mapping) is a planning aid used by practitioners, not a validated scientific model. The tool’s totals and quadrant suggestions are transparent arithmetic on your ratings and carry no predictive claim. The author’s read is one informed interpretation of a fictional case.

debrief.text: Most learners find that the decisive figures are not the most senior ones. In the author’s read, the sponsor and the quality officer are strong supporters, the hospitalist chair is the strongest opponent, and the change turns on three people with modest titles: the charge nurse who controls credibility on the units, the senior hospitalist who bridges the physician and nursing networks, and the informaticist who brokers between IT and the bedside. A plan that wins the executives and ignores them can produce a protocol that exists in policy and is rarely used — the ceremonial adoption risk from Lesson 3.

Look again at the opponents. The critical care director and the union steward oppose for reasons that are resolvable — capacity and blame — and their concerns improve the design. The hospitalist chair’s opposition rests partly on a real risk (fragmented care) and partly on lost decision rights. Offering him bounded influence over the physician notification step is a co-optation strategy with a clear line: he shapes how physicians are informed, not whether nurses may call.

**What this exercise does not show.** A static map cannot capture how stances shift once people see each other move, how much time each conversation costs, or how accurate your information is — in a real organization, profiles like these are themselves guesses. The grid is a practitioner heuristic for organizing thought, not a measurement. Use it to decide whom to talk to first and what to ask, then update it after every conversation.

assumptions: All people, the organization and the details of the protocol are fictional.
Power is rated for this specific change, not in general; the same person could rate differently on another decision.
Stances are current positions before any engagement; they are expected to move.
Ties listed are those known to the change sponsor; other ties exist and are unknown.
The power/interest grid is a practitioner heuristic; totals are simple arithmetic on ratings, not predictions.

case.title: The Office Nobody Owned
case.fiction: All people, organizations, places and data in this case are fictional. Numbers are synthetic and chosen for teaching.

body.text: On a Tuesday in early March, Renata Solís, deputy city manager of the City of Easterly Bend, received a two-paragraph memo from the newly elected mayor. Easterly Bend would create an **Office of Overdose Response** within ninety days. Its purpose was to connect people who survived an overdose with treatment within seventy-two hours. Solís would design it. The mayor had campaigned on the issue after a rise in overdose deaths, and her memo ended with a sentence Solís reread several times: “This should not belong to any one department. It should belong to the city.”

Solís had spent eleven years in city government and knew what an office that belonged to no department usually meant: an office with no budget line, no staff it could direct and no one obliged to return its calls. The work the mayor described crossed at least four organizations, and the city controlled only three of them.

The **Fire Department**, which runs the city’s emergency medical services, responded to every overdose call and knew within minutes who had survived. Fire Chief Walter Brandt had led the department for nine years and had served in it for thirty-one. His paramedics had for two years run a small, informal program in which two of them, on their own time, visited survivors who agreed to be contacted. Brandt was proud of it, protective of it, and skeptical of anything that might turn his paramedics into “social workers with a siren”. He also controlled the data: patient care reports were medical records held by his department, and his counsel had advised that sharing identifiable records with another agency required a formal agreement and, in some cases, the patient’s consent.

The **Department of Public Health**, led by Dr. Amara Nwosu, a physician two years into the job, had epidemiologists, a modest naloxone distribution program and the grant-writing capacity the city would need. Nwosu believed the office should sit in her department because overdose was a public-health problem. She had been quietly frustrated that Fire’s data reached her only as monthly totals. Her department’s most trusted link to Fire was an epidemiologist, Joel Haddad, who had worked as a paramedic for six years before graduate school; when the numbers looked strange, both departments called him.

The **Police Department** also responded to many overdose calls. Its chief, Leonard Pike, had told the council he supported “getting people help” but wanted officers to retain discretion over arrests at overdose scenes. The police union had publicly opposed a neighboring city’s policy of not arresting at such scenes. Several community advocates, including the founder of a peer-recovery group that had worked in the city for fifteen years, Marisol Reyes, said bluntly that survivors would not open the door to anyone they associated with police — and that Fire’s informal visits worked precisely because paramedics were not police.

The fourth organization was not the city’s at all. **Riverside County Behavioral Health**, a county agency, administered the publicly funded treatment slots on which any seventy-two-hour connection depended. Its director, Phyllis Garner, was cordial, overloaded and in no way accountable to the mayor. Treatment slots were limited, and the county’s board had its own priorities, including a long waiting list of people referred by the courts.

The city expected to receive a multiyear allocation from a legal settlement with opioid manufacturers and distributors (synthetic amount: about $2.4 million over four years, Exhibit 2). The council would have to approve any spending. Council member Theo Varga, who chaired the health committee, had made clear that he expected a “visible, measurable program” before the next budget cycle and that he was wary of the funds disappearing into existing departmental budgets. He also represented the district where the peer-recovery group worked and listened to Reyes.

By mid-April, three designs were circulating. **Design A**, favored by Nwosu, placed the office inside Public Health, with a director reporting to her, two outreach workers and a data-sharing agreement requiring Fire to send identifiable overdose reports within twenty-four hours. It was the cleanest structure. Brandt let it be known that he would “consider” a data agreement once he understood how his patients’ information would be protected, and that his paramedics’ visits would continue under Fire.

**Design B**, sketched by Brandt’s deputy, expanded the informal paramedic program into a formal unit within Fire, staffed by paramedics and one peer-recovery specialist, with Public Health providing data analysis and evaluation. It used Fire’s existing access to survivors and its credibility on the street. Nwosu objected that it would make a public-health program dependent on a department whose leadership regarded social services as outside its mission, and that Fire had never run an evaluation.

**Design C**, which Solís herself had begun to favor, created a small office in the city manager’s office with a director who chaired a standing working group of Fire, Public Health, Police and the county, and who held the settlement-funded budget. Outreach would be done by a team drawn from Fire paramedics and peer specialists from community organizations, with Public Health running evaluation. The office would own the money and the measures; the departments would own the work. Its weakness was the one Solís had recognized on the first day: the director would have budget but no authority over the people doing the work, and every department would retain the ability to slow it.

Solís convened the four leaders and Varga in late April. The meeting went worse than she had hoped. Nwosu argued that Design C was “a committee pretending to be an office”. Brandt said that if the office wanted his paramedics, it would need his department’s name on it. Pike said little except that police would continue to respond to overdose calls “as public safety requires”. Garner said the county could reserve perhaps a quarter of the slots the mayor’s target implied, and only if the city paid for a county care coordinator. Varga asked who, in any of these designs, the council could hold accountable if the numbers did not move.

Afterward, Haddad, the epidemiologist, stopped by Solís’s office. He said he thought Brandt would share data if Fire were treated as a partner rather than a supplier — “he has been running this on his own time for two years and nobody thanked him” — and that Fire’s paramedics trusted the peer-recovery group more than they trusted Public Health. He also said he was being asked by both departments to help and was not sure how long he could keep doing two jobs.

The mayor’s chief of staff called the next morning. The mayor wanted to announce the office at a press event in three weeks and would like the director named. Two candidates had been suggested: a respected Fire captain who had started the informal visits, and a Public Health program manager with a strong evaluation background. Solís had also been told, informally, that one council member would oppose any design that involved police at all and that another would oppose any design that did not.

Solís had five weeks before the ninety-day deadline, a budget that did not yet exist, data she could not compel, treatment capacity she did not control, and four leaders each of whom could make the office fail without ever saying no. She opened a blank page and wrote at the top: “Who has to win, who can afford to lose, and what am I not willing to trade?”

questions: Map the power in this case using dependence: what does each actor control that the office needs, how much discretion do they have, and what alternatives exist? Who are the hidden power holders?
Which design best balances effectiveness, legitimacy and the coalition needed to sustain it? What would you have to concede to make it work, and to whom?
Brandt’s support may require giving Fire visible ownership. Using Selznick’s analysis of co-optation, what would that buy, what could it cost, and where would you draw the line?
Joel Haddad is the only reliable bridge between Fire and Public Health. What are the risks of that structure, and what would you do about them in the first month?
Should Solís name a director before the press event? Whom, and how would each choice change the coalition?

perspectives.title: Build around the dependency: Fire-led with conditions
perspectives.text: Fire controls the two things the office cannot do without — access to survivors and their trust — and Brandt has a working program. A Design B variant, with a peer specialist from the community group, Public Health running evaluation under a written data agreement, and settlement funds released by the council against agreed measures, turns the strongest potential blocker into the owner. The risk is Selznick’s: Fire may narrow the mission to what paramedics are comfortable doing. The line is that evaluation and the outcome measures sit outside Fire and are reported publicly.

perspectives.title: Own the money and the measures: a small central office
perspectives.text: Design C is weak on authority but strong on legitimacy with the council and the advocates, and it avoids giving any single department a veto over a cross-cutting problem. Its success depends on the director’s ability to build exchange relationships — funding Fire’s visits, paying for the county coordinator, giving Public Health the evaluation role — so that each department gains something it values. Naming the Fire captain as director, with a Public Health deputy for evaluation, bridges the two networks. The risk is that a coordinating office without authority becomes ceremonial; the safeguard is a budget it actually controls and quarterly public results.

perspectives.title: Slow down: secure the county and the data first
perspectives.text: Every design fails if there are no treatment slots and no timely data. Announcing an office before those exist risks a visible program that cannot deliver, eroding legitimacy for years. On this view, Solís should recommend that the mayor announce a commitment and a working group, fund the county coordinator immediately, negotiate the data agreement with Fire as a partner, and name the director only when the design has the two dependencies in hand. The cost is political: the mayor wanted a launch, and delay may be read as weakness.

case.application: The same structure appears whenever a leader in a sports organization must introduce a process that crosses departments — for example a player-health and performance program that needs data from the medical staff, buy-in from coaches, budget from senior executives and cooperation from an international operation the department does not control. Map what each group controls, recognize who is already doing the work informally and deserves credit, decide which dependency must be secured before launch, and be explicit about what you will not trade for support. Do not let the pressure for a visible announcement substitute for the coalition that makes the process work.

questions.prompt: A newly appointed head of analytics at a hospital system has a vice-presidential title, but unit managers routinely route data questions to a long-tenured database administrator instead. In French and Raven’s terms, the head of analytics holds mainly which base of power over unit managers, and the administrator which?

options.text: Head: expert; administrator: legitimate.
Head: legitimate; administrator: expert.
Head: referent; administrator: coercive.
Head: reward; administrator: referent.

questions.explanation: The title confers legitimate power — an accepted right to direct. Unit managers go to the administrator because they believe she knows more about the data, which is expert power. The gap between the two is the gap between formal authority and practical power this week examines.

optionFeedback.a: This reverses the bases: the title is the legitimate base; being consulted for knowledge is expert.
optionFeedback.c: Nothing suggests identification with the head or that the administrator can punish anyone.
optionFeedback.d: Reward power would require control over things managers value; referent power would require identification. Neither is described.

questions.prompt: Using the ratings in the table, what share of the power held by people who have taken a side (stance not 0) belongs to supporters? Give a percentage to one decimal place.

stimulus.caption: Stakeholder ratings for a proposed change (synthetic)

questions.working: Supporters (stance above 0): A (5) and C (3), total 8. Opponents (stance below 0): B (4) and D (2), total 6. Committed power = 8 + 6 = 14. Supporters’ share = 8 / 14 = 0.571 = 57.1%. E (power 4, neutral) is excluded — and is the largest swing factor: if E opposed, the share would fall to 8 / 18 = 44.4%.
questions.explanation: Supporters hold 8 of the 14 points of committed power, or 57.1%. The more important observation is that a single high-power neutral, E, could reverse the balance, which is why stakeholder maps flag powerful neutrals for early engagement.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the weak-ties research are supported by the evidence discussed this week? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bridges between dense clusters tend to be weak ties, so weak ties tend to carry information that is new to a group.
A randomized test on a professional networking platform found that the weaker a tie, the more it helped job mobility, without limit.
The randomized test found an inverted-U pattern in which moderately weak ties were most helpful for job mobility.
Granovetter’s original job-search evidence was descriptive rather than causal.
The randomized test showed that strong ties are useless in every industry.

questions.explanation: Granovetter’s structural argument explains why bridges are weak ties and why they carry novel information; his own evidence was descriptive. The LinkedIn experiments provided causal evidence but found an inverted U, and weak ties mattered more in more digital industries — not that strong ties are useless.

optionFeedback.b: The study found diminishing and then reversing returns: the weakest ties were less helpful than moderately weak ones.
optionFeedback.e: Strong ties were relatively more valuable in less digital industries.

questions.prompt: Which is the most important structural risk, and the best first response?

stimulus.text: A global consulting firm’s Latin American and U.S. healthcare practices share clients but rarely work together. One bilingual principal, Andrés, has worked in both and is the person each practice calls when it needs the other. Joint proposals have doubled since he took on this role. He has just been approached by a competitor. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Andrés is a broker whose role creates a single bridge between groups — a bottleneck and a memory risk. Build additional ties between the practices and capture what he knows, while recognizing and rewarding his role.
Andrés is too central in the trust network; reduce his involvement so that the practices learn to work alone.
The practices are too densely connected; separate them further to protect their distinct cultures.
The risk is purely financial; counter the competitor’s offer and change nothing else.

questions.explanation: Andrés spans a structural hole; the doubling of joint proposals is consistent with the value of brokerage. But a single bridge is fragile: if he leaves, so do the paths along which cross-practice knowledge travels. Retaining him may be wise, but the structural fix is redundancy plus recognition.

optionFeedback.b: Reducing his role removes the value he creates without building an alternative bridge.
optionFeedback.c: The problem is too few ties between the practices, not too many.
optionFeedback.d: A counteroffer may be sensible, but it leaves the organization exposed to the same single-point failure next time.

questions.prompt: Identify the central weakness in this argument.

stimulus.text: “Eight of the ten largest health systems in our region have created a Chief Experience Officer in the past three years. We are falling behind. The board should approve the role this quarter so that we are seen as a modern organization by patients and regulators.”

options.text: It provides no evidence that the role improves outcomes in the systems that adopted it; adopting it because peers have it is mimetic isomorphism, which risks a ceremonial role.
It relies on coercive pressure from regulators, which is illegitimate.
It ignores that the role is too expensive for any health system.
It assumes that patients care about organizational structure, which they never do.

questions.explanation: The argument treats peer adoption as sufficient reason. That is the signature of mimetic isomorphism under uncertainty. Legitimacy has real value, but the question the board should ask is what the role would change and how that would be checked, so that the organization adopts the function rather than only the form.

optionFeedback.b: No regulatory mandate is cited; “seen as modern” is about legitimacy, not coercion. Coercive pressure is not inherently illegitimate either.
optionFeedback.c: Cost is not discussed in the argument and may be justified; the flaw is the missing evidence of effect.
optionFeedback.d: An absolute claim of this kind is unsupported; the flaw lies in the reasoning from peer adoption.

questions.prompt: A county is merging its housing-inspection and code-enforcement units. The code-enforcement manager, respected by council members, opposes the merger because inspectors will report to a housing director. Rank these responses from best to worst, considering support gained, mission protection and trust.

options.text: Invite the manager to lead the design of the merged unit’s field procedures and cross-training, while the reporting line and service standards remain fixed and published.
Give the manager an honorary title on the transition steering committee, which has no decision rights.
Proceed without engaging the manager and ask council members to stay neutral.
Let the manager decide the reporting line in exchange for public support.

questions.explanation: Bounded informal co-optation (a) gives real influence over matters that can be conceded while protecting the core purpose. Symbolic participation (b) buys little but costs little. Ignoring a respected opponent (c) invites quiet obstruction through council allies. Handing over the reporting line (d) buys support with the mission itself — the outcome Selznick warned about.

questions.prompt: From the coalition perspective, what is the most useful interpretation of the planners’ resistance, and the best next step?

stimulus.text: A regional airline introduces a new crew-scheduling optimization system. Senior schedulers, who have long had informal discretion to swap shifts for crews they know well, raise repeated technical objections and delay training. The project lead calls them “resistant to change”. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: The schedulers fear technology; schedule more training until they are comfortable.

The system removes a side payment — discretion that gives schedulers status and goodwill with crews — and their objections may also contain real information about constraints the system ignores. Find out what the discretion did, and redesign or compensate for what is legitimate.
The objections are purely self-interested; escalate to senior management and mandate use.
Resistance shows the system is flawed; cancel the project.

questions.explanation: In the coalition view, resistance often defends a threatened bargain. Here the bargain is informal discretion, which also served crews and may encode constraints the optimizer misses. Treating resistance as information separates the principled part (constraints) from the self-interested part (lost status), and lets you address each.

optionFeedback.a: Training addresses skill, not lost discretion; this misdiagnoses the cause.
optionFeedback.c: Mandating may win compliance but forfeits the information in the objections and damages trust with people the system still depends on.
optionFeedback.d: Resistance is information, not a verdict; it does not by itself show the system is flawed.

questions.prompt: You want your organization’s chief executive to prioritize a data-privacy weakness you have identified. She is focused this quarter on a large customer renewal. Using Dutton and Ashford’s framework, what is the best first move?

options.text: Raise it at the next all-leaders meeting so that the issue is on the record.
Frame the weakness in terms of the renewal — for example the customer’s security review — and raise it first in a private conversation, with a peer whose function is affected ready to co-sponsor.
Wait until the renewal is complete so as not to distract her.
Send a detailed technical memo to the whole executive team.

questions.explanation: Packaging links the issue to a goal the executive owns; process chooses a private first channel (reducing her surprise and your image risk) and involves an ally. Timing matters too: tying the issue to the renewal turns a distraction into a contribution.

optionFeedback.a: A public first raising risks surprising the executive in front of others and raises your image risk.
optionFeedback.c: Waiting may be wise for some issues, but here the issue can be framed as relevant to the current priority; delay forgoes the window.
optionFeedback.d: A technical memo to everyone ignores framing and channel and is likely to be read as alarmism or ignored.

questions.prompt: In Yukl and Tracey’s field study, which tactics were most associated with target commitment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rational persuasion
Pressure
Inspirational appeals
Legitimating tactics
Consultation
Coalition tactics

questions.explanation: Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation were most associated with commitment. Pressure, legitimating and coalition tactics were least effective. Remember that the study was correlational: tactic choice partly reflects expected resistance.

optionFeedback.b: Pressure was among the least effective tactics.
optionFeedback.d: Appeals to rules or authority were among the least effective.
optionFeedback.f: Using others to pressure the target was among the least effective — different from building a coalition behind a proposal.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest alternative explanation for this finding?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract. In a survey of 310 project managers, those who reported using pressure tactics with peers were rated by those peers as less effective, and their projects were more often late. The authors conclude that pressure tactics cause project delays and recommend training managers to avoid them.

options.text: Managers may resort to pressure on projects that are already in trouble or facing resistance, so delays and pressure could share a cause or delays could cause pressure.
The sample is too small for any conclusion.
Peers cannot rate managers’ effectiveness accurately.
Pressure tactics are effective, so the finding must be wrong.

questions.explanation: Tactic choice is endogenous: managers choose pressure when they already expect resistance or are behind schedule. The correlation fits the hypothesis that pressure causes delay but equally fits reverse causation and confounding. The training recommendation may still be reasonable on other grounds, but this design cannot establish it.

optionFeedback.b: Three hundred respondents is a reasonable sample; size is not the main problem.
optionFeedback.c: Peer ratings carry bias but are informative; this is a weaker objection than reverse causation.
optionFeedback.d: This asserts the opposite conclusion without evidence.

questions.prompt: In 150–250 words: a regional hospital’s new chief operating officer wants to centralize operating-room scheduling, which surgical department chiefs have controlled for years. The surgeons’ informal leader is a senior surgeon with no administrative title, central in the surgeons’ trust network. Outline an engagement strategy that uses at least three ideas from this week (dependence, networks, coalitions/co-optation, influence tactics, ethics), states what the COO should be willing to concede and what not, and names one ethical line.
questions.modelAnswer: The COO should begin by mapping dependence: the hospital depends on surgeons for revenue and on the department chiefs for schedule adherence, while chiefs depend on the COO’s office for staffing and equipment. Centralization removes a side payment — chiefs’ discretion over OR time, a source of status and leverage — so resistance is predictable and partly rational. The senior surgeon is a hidden power holder: no title, but control over the credibility of the change among surgeons. The COO should consult him early, privately, with data on idle OR time and delays, framed around patient access and surgeons’ own frustrations. A bounded co-optation is appropriate: invite him and two chiefs to design the allocation rules and the appeals process, while keeping centralized scheduling, published utilization data and the final authority fixed. The COO can concede block-time protections for high-volume surgeons and a phased start; not the principle of centralized, transparent allocation. Tactics should favor rational persuasion and consultation over legitimating appeals (“the board decided”). Ethical line: no selective sharing of data to make particular chiefs look bad, and no private promises of OR time in exchange for public support.

rubric.criterion: Diagnosis of power and dependence (including the hidden power holder)
levels: 2 — Identifies dependence or the informal leader
3 — Specific dependence analysis and the informal leader’s source of power

rubric.criterion: Coalition strategy with explicit concessions and limits
levels: 3 — Bounded co-optation: what is conceded and what is not
2 — Favors commitment-producing tactics, with a reason
2 — Specific, testable line tied to the situation

reserve.prompt: According to resource dependence theory, which change would most reduce a product team’s dependence on a single cloud vendor?

options.text: Praising the vendor’s account manager publicly.
Developing the capability to run critical workloads on a second provider.
Increasing the product team’s budget.
Appointing a senior executive to manage the vendor relationship.

reserve.explanation: Dependence rises with importance, the other party’s discretion and the scarcity of alternatives. Creating an alternative source is the most direct way to reduce it. The other options may improve the relationship but leave the dependence intact.

optionFeedback.a: Goodwill may help the relationship but does not change the structure of dependence.
optionFeedback.c: More budget does not create alternatives on its own.
optionFeedback.d: Seniority may help negotiation but leaves importance, discretion and alternatives unchanged.

reserve.prompt: What does Krackhardt and Hanson’s framework suggest the director should do first?

stimulus.text: A research hospital’s new laboratory director wants to introduce a new specimen-tracking procedure. She asks for a list of “key influencers” and is given the five most senior technologists. Two months later the procedure is followed inconsistently. Informal conversations reveal that technologists on every shift ask a mid-career technologist, Mei, how to handle unusual cases, and that night staff confide problems in a phlebotomy supervisor, Tomás. (Hypothetical.)

options.text: Re-train the five senior technologists more intensively.
Recognize that seniority approximated neither the advice nor the trust network; engage Mei (advice) and Tomás (trust) in revising and championing the procedure.
Issue a written directive requiring compliance.
Conduct a large network survey before taking any action.

reserve.explanation: The informal advice network runs through Mei and the trust network through Tomás. Seniority is a formal attribute that may not coincide with either. Engaging those who are actually consulted and trusted is the most direct way to make the procedure credible.

optionFeedback.a: The problem is not the seniors’ skill; they are not where advice and trust flow.
optionFeedback.c: A directive relies on legitimate power and may yield compliance without commitment.
optionFeedback.d: A survey can help but is slow; the conversations already reveal the key figures.

reserve.prompt: In Cyert and March’s behavioral theory of the firm, what role does organizational slack play?

options.text: It is waste that efficient organizations eliminate entirely.
It provides surplus resources that allow the organization to satisfy several coalition members’ demands at once, easing conflict.
It is the time managers spend on informal networking.
It is the gap between legitimate and expert power.

reserve.explanation: Slack is surplus beyond what is strictly needed. In the coalition view, it lets the organization make side payments to several members simultaneously, which keeps the coalition together. When slack shrinks, conflicts become harder to manage, which is one reason change during budget cuts is so politically difficult.

optionFeedback.a: Slack may look like waste, but Cyert and March showed it serves a political function.
optionFeedback.c: This is not the meaning of slack.
optionFeedback.d: This confuses concepts from different lessons.

reserve.prompt: A colleague suggests opening a budget discussion with a deliberately inflated request you expect to be refused, so that your real request seems reasonable by comparison, and not telling the finance director this is the plan. Which response best reflects this week’s treatment of influence?

options.text: Use it: the door-in-the-face technique replicated, so it will work.

Decline: it fails the disclosure test in a repeated relationship, and if the finance director recognizes the tactic, the trust cost may exceed the gain. Make the real request with reasons and offer options.
Use it, but only with peers, because influence tactics work better laterally.
Decline because door-in-the-face has been shown not to replicate.

reserve.explanation: A staged concession only works if hidden, so it fails the disclosure test. In repeated relationships, recognition damages trust. The replication evidence concerns whether the technique works with strangers, not whether it is wise or ethical with a colleague.

optionFeedback.a: Replication with strangers does not settle effect size or consequences in a repeated relationship, nor the ethical question.
optionFeedback.c: The finance director is not clearly a peer, and direction does not resolve the ethical problem.
optionFeedback.d: This misstates the evidence: the door-in-the-face technique replicated well in a direct replication.

assignment.title: Stakeholder Engagement Plan

brief.text: Write a stakeholder engagement plan for introducing a change initiative of your choosing. The default is the owner’s brief for this week: **a new analytical or operational process in a professional sports organization**, with particular attention to implementing the improvement without undermining existing relationships. You may instead choose a change in another kind of organization. The initiative must be non-confidential: describe a hypothetical or generalized situation, use roles rather than names, and include no proprietary data or details that would identify a real organization or person.

Your plan should read like a working document a senior leader could actually use: specific about people (by role), dependencies and sequence; honest about uncertainty; and explicit about what you will and will not do to win support. Use the week’s tools — dependence, networks, coalitions and legitimacy, influence tactics — and label any practitioner heuristic (such as a power/interest grid) as a heuristic.

items: Treat existing relationships as assets the change must protect: name which ones and how your plan protects them.
Distinguish what you know about each stakeholder from what you are assuming, and say how you will test the assumptions.
Prefer tactics associated with commitment; justify any use of pressure or appeals to authority.
State your ethical lines concretely enough that someone could tell whether you crossed them.

assignment.deliverable: A 1,200–1,800-word stakeholder engagement plan with the eight sections below, including a stakeholder map (table or grid) of 6–12 roles.

template.heading: Objective and the change
template.guidance: In 100–150 words: what will change, for whom, by when, and what success looks like in behavior, not only in approval. State why the change is worth its political cost.

template.heading: Stakeholder map
template.guidance: A table of 6–12 roles with power over this change (and its source: what do they control, with what discretion and alternatives?), interest, current stance, and what each gains or loses. Mark hidden power holders and known ties. Label the power/interest grid as a practitioner heuristic.

template.heading: Relationships to protect
template.guidance: Which existing relationships — between people, departments or with outside partners — carry trust or institutional memory the change depends on? How could the change damage them, and how will your plan avoid that?

template.heading: Coalition strategy
template.guidance: Who must be part of the winning coalition, who can be kept satisfied, and who will remain opposed? Which brokers or trusted figures will you work through? If you co-opt anyone, what influence do they get and over what?

template.heading: Sequencing of conversations
template.guidance: The order of your first 6–10 conversations, with the purpose of each, the tactic you will lead with, and what you need to learn. Explain why the order matters (who must not be surprised; whose early support changes others’ calculations).

template.heading: Concessions and their limits
template.guidance: What you are prepared to give — timing, design input, credit, resources, pilots — and what is non-negotiable because it is the purpose of the change. Tie each concession to a stakeholder interest.

template.heading: Risks and early warning signs
template.guidance: Three to five specific risks (for example ceremonial adoption, a broker’s departure, a sponsor’s exit, passive resistance) with an observable early signal and a response for each.

template.heading: Ethical lines
template.guidance: Two to four concrete commitments about how you will and will not influence people (for example the disclosure test, no selective use of data, no private promises), and how you would handle a conflict between winning support and keeping them.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Power is analyzed through specific dependencies (importance, discretion, alternatives) and bases; hidden power holders are identified and justified; known facts are separated from assumptions.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Sources of power are identified for most stakeholders beyond titles; at least one informal power holder is recognized.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Power is mostly read from titles; dependencies are mentioned in general terms.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Stakeholders are listed without analysis of where their power comes from.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Uses advice and trust networks, brokers and single bridges; the coalition strategy is explicit about side payments and any co-optation, with its limits.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Identifies key relationships and a credible coalition; co-optation, if used, is bounded.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Coalition is described as “get buy-in” without specifying who, why or at what price.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No coalition logic; the plan relies on authority or announcement.

rubric.criterion: Sequencing and influence tactics grounded in evidence

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A reasoned order of conversations with purposes and tactics; favors commitment-producing tactics, adapts to direction (up, lateral, down) and culture, and justifies any exceptions.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear sequence and appropriate tactics for most conversations.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Sequence present but unexplained, or tactics generic.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No sequence; tactics absent or pressure-led.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Concessions are tied to specific interests, with a clear non-negotiable core; the plan names the relationships at stake and protects them concretely.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Concessions and limits are stated; relationships are considered.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Concessions vague or unlimited; relationships mentioned only in passing.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No concessions or no attention to existing relationships.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Specific risks with observable signals and responses; concrete, testable ethical lines; practitioner heuristics labelled as such; uncertainty acknowledged.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Risks and ethical lines are specific; most claims are appropriately qualified.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Risks generic; ethical lines stated as general values.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Risks or ethics missing; heuristics presented as science.

prompts: Think of a change you championed that was adopted on paper but not in practice. Using this week’s tools, who held the practical power over adoption, and did you engage them?
Where in your own network are you a broker — across departments, languages, countries or professions? What does that position give you, and what does it oblige you to do for the people on each side?
Which influence tactic do you reach for first under time pressure, and what does the evidence suggest it costs you?
Write down one influence approach you have used or seen used that you would not want disclosed to its target. What would you do differently now?

review.front: What are French and Raven’s five original bases of power, and from whose perspective is each defined?
review.back: Reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert — each defined by the target’s beliefs about the agent. Raven later added informational power.

review.front: State the power-dependence principle and the three conditions that increase dependence.
review.back: A’s power over B equals B’s dependence on A. Dependence rises with the importance of the resource, A’s discretion over it, and the scarcity of alternatives.

review.front: Name three ways organizations manage external dependence, according to resource dependence theory.
review.back: Co-opting outsiders (e.g. onto boards), alliances and joint ventures, mergers, and diversifying sources of the resource.
Someone with little formal authority who controls a critical dependency for a specific decision — for example credibility with front-line staff — and can therefore make or break a change.

review.front: Why are bridges between groups almost always weak ties?
review.back: Strong ties pull people’s contacts together, so two strongly tied clusters would merge; the ties that remain between separate clusters are weak, and they carry non-redundant information.

review.front: What did the randomized LinkedIn study find about weak ties and job mobility?
review.back: A causal effect with an inverted-U shape: moderately weak ties helped most; the weakest ties helped less. Weak ties mattered more in more digital industries.

review.front: What is a structural hole, and what did Burt find about brokers who span them?
review.back: A gap between unconnected groups. In one electronics firm, brokers’ ideas were more often judged valuable, and brokerage was associated with pay, evaluations and promotion — an observational finding.

review.front: Distinguish the advice network from the trust network.
review.back: Advice: whom people ask for technical help. Trust: with whom they share sensitive information and whom they back in a crisis. A change needs the trusted as well as the expert.

review.front: In Cyert and March’s view, how is an organization held together despite conflicting goals?
review.back: By bargaining among coalition members, side payments, organizational slack and sequential attention to different goals; conflict is managed, not resolved.

review.front: Name and define the three mechanisms of institutional isomorphism.
review.back: Coercive (pressure from those depended on and the state), mimetic (copying peers under uncertainty), normative (professional training and associations).

review.front: What is the hidden cost of co-optation in Selznick’s TVA study?
review.back: Interests brought into the decision structure gain leverage over the organization’s real commitments, so support can be bought at the price of drift from the mission.

review.front: What is ceremonial adoption, and when is it most likely?
review.back: Adopting the visible form of a practice without changing the underlying work; most likely when adoption is driven by legitimacy (mimetic or coercive pressure) rather than evidence of results.

review.front: Which influence tactics were most and least associated with commitment in Yukl and Tracey’s study?
review.back: Most: rational persuasion, inspirational appeals, consultation. Least: pressure, legitimating, coalition. Ingratiation and exchange worked with peers and subordinates, not bosses.

review.front: What are the two levers of an issue-selling attempt in Dutton and Ashford’s framework?
review.back: Packaging (framing, bundling with leaders’ concerns) and process (timing, channel, involving others) — with image risk shaping whether people try at all.

review.front: Summarize the replication picture for compliance principles in one sentence.
review.back: The principles name real mechanisms and some classic effects (e.g. door-in-the-face) replicate well, but many specific effect sizes are smaller or less certain than early studies suggested, especially for repeated relationships.

review.front: State the disclosure test for influence.
review.back: Would the approach still work, and would you still be comfortable, if the target knew exactly what you were doing and why? If not, it is probably manipulation.

preview.text: This week’s map of power becomes next week’s bargaining table. In Week 7, leverage in negotiation turns out to be dependence again — your alternatives set your power — and the ethics of influence return as negotiation ethics. Week 8 moves from the informal architecture to the formal one: designing structures, decision rights and incentives that create or dissolve the coalitions you studied here. Week 12 puts both together in implementing change, where the stakeholder engagement plan you write this week becomes the first section of a 90-day roadmap.

links.why: Bargaining power, alternatives and negotiation ethics build directly on dependence and influence tactics.
Formal organizational design allocates the authority and creates the coalitions analyzed this week.
Change implementation uses stakeholder mapping, sequencing and coalition-building at scale.
Governance and ethics revisit legitimacy, co-optation and the ethics of influence.
